He denied weight loss, fever, night sweats, cough, or hemoptysis. He had a history of coronary artery disease with prior coronary artery bypass grafting, peripheral vascular disease, abdominal aortic aneurysm repair, and ulcerative colitis. He reported no immunosuppressive therapy. He quit smoking 8 months prior after a 35–pack-year history and consumed alcohol infrequently. He denied recent travel, exposure to tuberculosis, or prior radiation to the head and neck. On physical examination, there were no palpable cervical lymph nodes or oropharyngeal abnormalities. Flexible laryngoscopy revealed a fibrinous, ulcerative lesion on the laryngeal surface of the epiglottis with surrounding edema and preserved bilateral vocal cord mobility. Given concern for cancer, the patient underwent direct laryngoscopy and biopsy. Examination under anesthesia confirmed irregular mucosa with fibrinous exudate localized to the epiglottis. Histopathology results revealed necrotizing and nonnecrotizing granulomatous inflammation with multinucleated giant cells (Figure, A). Grocott methenamine silver stain highlighted narrow-based budding yeast (Figure, B).

case_info.explanation: Laryngeal histoplasmosis is a rare extrapulmonary manifestation ofHistoplasma capsulatum, a dimorphic fungus endemic to the Ohio and Mississippi river valleys. While histoplasmosis typically presents as a self-limited pulmonary illness, it may disseminate and affect extrapulmonary organs, including the larynx, even in immunocompetent individuals.1In this case, a man with no overt immunosuppression developed ulcerative supraglottic disease mimicking cancer, ultimately diagnosed by fungal staining on biopsy. Endoscopic features of laryngeal histoplasmosis can closely resemble squamous cell carcinoma, with ulcerative lesions, irregular mucosa, or masslike findings localized to the epiglottis, aryepiglottic folds, or vocal cords.2The overlap in appearance frequently leads to initial diagnostic concern for cancer, particularly in older adults with a history of tobacco use.3,4However, histopathologic evaluation remains the criterion standard for diagnosis. Histology results typically reveal necrotizing and nonnecrotizing granulomatous inflammation with multinucleated giant cells and fungal organisms.5,6Grocott methenamine silver or periodic acid–Schiff staining identifies the characteristic small, oval intracellular yeasts ofH capsulatum. In this case, the biopsy lacked dysplasia or neoplasia but demonstrated abundant submucosal nonnecrotizing granulomatous inflammation and multinucleated giant cell formation with fungal organisms consistent withH capsulatum. A serum histoplasma antigen level was then obtained and returned positive at 1.95 ng/mL, supporting the diagnosis and prompting antifungal therapy. Alternative considerations include laryngeal tuberculosis (TB), which may also present with hoarseness, mucosal ulceration, and granulomatous inflammation. However, TB is identified by acid-fast bacilli on staining or culture.4In this patient, no acid-fast bacilli were found, and fungal organisms were clearly demonstrated. Chronic laryngitis, another consideration in those who smoke, does not typically cause ulceration or granulomas and lacks fungal or mycobacterial organisms.1 Imaging studies are generally nonspecific but may support the extent of involvement. In this case, imaging was not diagnostic. The patient’s location in the Ohio River Valley served as an epidemiologic clue. Inhalation of microconidia from contaminated soil, often associated with bird or bat droppings, is the primary route of exposure.3While disseminated disease is more common in immunocompromised patients, it may also occur in older or chronically ill individuals without overt immunodeficiency. The treatment of laryngeal histoplasmosis is guided by the Infectious Diseases Society of America. For moderate to severe disease, the Infectious Diseases Society of America recommends liposomal amphotericin B at 3.0 mg/kg/d for 1 to 2 weeks, followed by oral itraconazole at 200 mg twice daily for at least 12 months.7For mild to moderate cases, itraconazole may be sufficient alone. In cases where immunosuppression cannot be reversed, long-term suppressive therapy may be necessary.8,9 This patient received a 2-week course of intravenous liposomal amphotericin B followed by a prolonged course of oral amphotericin B, as recommended by the infectious team. He also experienced 2 transient ischemic attacks during hospitalization, likely from a septic origin, and began anticoagulation with warfarin. His hoarseness and odynophagia improved considerably within 1 month. At 3-month follow-up, he remained symptom free. The initial delay in diagnosis underscores the importance of including fungal infections in the differential diagnosis of ulcerative laryngeal lesions, particularly in endemic areas. Laryngeal histoplasmosis is an important clinical mimic of squamous cell carcinoma and TB, and early biopsy with fungal staining is critical for accurate diagnosis. Prompt antifungal therapy can prevent complications such as airway obstruction, systemic dissemination, or unnecessary oncologic intervention. This case reinforces the need for clinicians to maintain suspicion for histoplasmosis in patients with chronic hoarseness and supraglottic lesions, even in the absence of overt immunosuppression.

case_info.explanation: Laryngeal histoplasmosis is a rare extrapulmonary manifestation ofHistoplasma capsulatum, a dimorphic fungus endemic to the Ohio and Mississippi river valleys. While histoplasmosis typically presents as a self-limited pulmonary illness, it may disseminate and affect extrapulmonary organs, including the larynx, even in immunocompetent individuals.1In this case, a man with no overt immunosuppression developed ulcerative supraglottic disease mimicking cancer, ultimately diagnosed by fungal staining on biopsy. Endoscopic features of laryngeal histoplasmosis can closely resemble squamous cell carcinoma, with ulcerative lesions, irregular mucosa, or masslike findings localized to the epiglottis, aryepiglottic folds, or vocal cords.2The overlap in appearance frequently leads to initial diagnostic concern for cancer, particularly in older adults with a history of tobacco use.3,4However, histopathologic evaluation remains the criterion standard for diagnosis. Histology results typically reveal necrotizing and nonnecrotizing granulomatous inflammation with multinucleated giant cells and fungal organisms.5,6Grocott methenamine silver or periodic acid–Schiff staining identifies the characteristic small, oval intracellular yeasts ofH capsulatum. In this case, the biopsy lacked dysplasia or neoplasia but demonstrated abundant submucosal nonnecrotizing granulomatous inflammation and multinucleated giant cell formation with fungal organisms consistent withH capsulatum. A serum histoplasma antigen level was then obtained and returned positive at 1.95 ng/mL, supporting the diagnosis and prompting antifungal therapy. Alternative considerations include laryngeal tuberculosis (TB), which may also present with hoarseness, mucosal ulceration, and granulomatous inflammation. However, TB is identified by acid-fast bacilli on staining or culture.4In this patient, no acid-fast bacilli were found, and fungal organisms were clearly demonstrated. Chronic laryngitis, another consideration in those who smoke, does not typically cause ulceration or granulomas and lacks fungal or mycobacterial organisms.1 Imaging studies are generally nonspecific but may support the extent of involvement. In this case, imaging was not diagnostic. The patient’s location in the Ohio River Valley served as an epidemiologic clue. Inhalation of microconidia from contaminated soil, often associated with bird or bat droppings, is the primary route of exposure.3While disseminated disease is more common in immunocompromised patients, it may also occur in older or chronically ill individuals without overt immunodeficiency. The treatment of laryngeal histoplasmosis is guided by the Infectious Diseases Society of America. For moderate to severe disease, the Infectious Diseases Society of America recommends liposomal amphotericin B at 3.0 mg/kg/d for 1 to 2 weeks, followed by oral itraconazole at 200 mg twice daily for at least 12 months.7For mild to moderate cases, itraconazole may be sufficient alone. He also experienced 2 transient ischemic attacks during hospitalization, likely from a septic origin, and began anticoagulation with warfarin. His hoarseness and odynophagia improved considerably within 1 month. At 3-month follow-up, he remained symptom free. The initial delay in diagnosis underscores the importance of including fungal infections in the differential diagnosis of ulcerative laryngeal lesions, particularly in endemic areas. Laryngeal histoplasmosis is an important clinical mimic of squamous cell carcinoma and TB, and early biopsy with fungal staining is critical for accurate diagnosis. Prompt antifungal therapy can prevent complications such as airway obstruction, systemic dissemination, or unnecessary oncologic intervention. This case reinforces the need for clinicians to maintain suspicion for histoplasmosis in patients with chronic hoarseness and supraglottic lesions, even in the absence of overt immunosuppression.

case_info.explanation: Laryngeal histoplasmosis is a rare extrapulmonary manifestation ofHistoplasma capsulatum, a dimorphic fungus endemic to the Ohio and Mississippi river valleys. While histoplasmosis typically presents as a self-limited pulmonary illness, it may disseminate and affect extrapulmonary organs, including the larynx, even in immunocompetent individuals.1In this case, a man with no overt immunosuppression developed ulcerative supraglottic disease mimicking cancer, ultimately diagnosed by fungal staining on biopsy. Endoscopic features of laryngeal histoplasmosis can closely resemble squamous cell carcinoma, with ulcerative lesions, irregular mucosa, or masslike findings localized to the epiglottis, aryepiglottic folds, or vocal cords.2The overlap in appearance frequently leads to initial diagnostic concern for cancer, particularly in older adults with a history of tobacco use.3,4However, histopathologic evaluation remains the criterion standard for diagnosis. Histology results typically reveal necrotizing and nonnecrotizing granulomatous inflammation with multinucleated giant cells and fungal organisms.5,6Grocott methenamine silver or periodic acid–Schiff staining identifies the characteristic small, oval intracellular yeasts ofH capsulatum. In this case, the biopsy lacked dysplasia or neoplasia but demonstrated abundant submucosal nonnecrotizing granulomatous inflammation and multinucleated giant cell formation with fungal organisms consistent withH capsulatum. A serum histoplasma antigen level was then obtained and returned positive at 1.95 ng/mL, supporting the diagnosis and prompting antifungal therapy. Alternative considerations include laryngeal tuberculosis (TB), which may also present with hoarseness, mucosal ulceration, and granulomatous inflammation. However, TB is identified by acid-fast bacilli on staining or culture.4In this patient, no acid-fast bacilli were found, and fungal organisms were clearly demonstrated. Chronic laryngitis, another consideration in those who smoke, does not typically cause ulceration or granulomas and lacks fungal or mycobacterial organisms.1 Imaging studies are generally nonspecific but may support the extent of involvement. In this case, imaging was not diagnostic. The patient’s location in the Ohio River Valley served as an epidemiologic clue. Inhalation of microconidia from contaminated soil, often associated with bird or bat droppings, is the primary route of exposure.3While disseminated disease is more common in immunocompromised patients, it may also occur in older or chronically ill individuals without overt immunodeficiency. The treatment of laryngeal histoplasmosis is guided by the Infectious Diseases Society of America. For moderate to severe disease, the Infectious Diseases Society of America recommends liposomal amphotericin B at 3.0 mg/kg/d for 1 to 2 weeks, followed by oral itraconazole at 200 mg twice daily for at least 12 months.7For mild to moderate cases, itraconazole may be sufficient alone. In cases where immunosuppression cannot be reversed, long-term suppressive therapy may be necessary.8,9 This patient received a 2-week course of intravenous liposomal amphotericin B followed by a prolonged course of oral amphotericin B, as recommended by the infectious team. He also experienced 2 transient ischemic attacks during hospitalization, likely from a septic origin, and began anticoagulation with warfarin. His hoarseness and odynophagia improved considerably within 1 month. At 3-month follow-up, he remained symptom free. The initial delay in diagnosis underscores the importance of including fungal infections in the differential diagnosis of ulcerative laryngeal lesions, particularly in endemic areas. Laryngeal histoplasmosis is an important clinical mimic of squamous cell carcinoma and TB, and early biopsy with fungal staining is critical for accurate diagnosis. Prompt antifungal therapy can prevent complications such as airway obstruction, systemic dissemination, or unnecessary oncologic intervention. This case reinforces the need for clinicians to maintain suspicion for histoplasmosis in patients with chronic hoarseness and supraglottic lesions, even in the absence of overt immunosuppression.

Case:
A 13-year-old male presented with a 7-month history of a painless, progressively enlarging mass in the right parotid region. He underwent surgery at a local hospital 6 months prior. The pathological diagnosis was lymphadenitis. However, the mass persistently enlarged after the surgery. When the patient visited our hospital, a bulging mass (approximately 5 × 4 cm) was palpable in the right parotid region, which was firm, nontender, and immobile. Contrast-enhanced maxillofacial computed tomography showed an ill-defined 3.6 × 3.2 × 2.7-cm soft-tissue mass in the superficial lobe of the right parotid gland, with indistinct borders at the posterior margin of the right masseter muscle. Multiple mildly enlarged lymph nodes were noted at the inferior pole of the parotid gland and adjacent to the superior margin of the lesion (Figure 1A). The patient underwent right parotid mass resection and total parotidectomy with facial nerve dissection. Intraoperative findings indicated a firm mass located within the superficial parotid lobe. It had adhered to the surface of the mandibular ramus, with indistinct planes of dissection from the masseter and temporalis muscles. Histopathology results demonstrated that a circumscribed mass was surrounded by a thick fibrous pseudocapsule, and the tumor was composed of epithelioid and spindle cells arranged in a multinodular and fascicular pattern. Pseudoangiomatoid spaces and a characteristic lymphoplasmacytic cuff were noted. The tumor showed focal sclerosing changes and no evidence of necrosis. Tumor cells appeared as mild atypia, while mitoses were rarely identified (Figure 1B). Immunostaining showed desmin, CD99, ALK D5F3, and cyclin D1 positivity.

Image Explanation:
A, Computed tomography showing a soft-tissue mass in the superficial lobe of the right parotid gland with ill-defined margins. B, Low-powered stain of a multinodular lesion containing multiple blood-filled spaces, surrounded by dense inflammatory cell infiltration and encased within a thick fibrous capsule (original magnification ×20).

[Question]
What is the most appropriate next step in management?

[Conversation so far]
[Doctor]: Given the clinical history of a recurrent, locally invasive parotid mass, the histopathology showing a circumscribed lesion with a thick pseudocapsule, and the specific immunoprofile (positive for desmin, CD99, ALK, and cyclin D1), the diagnosis is clearly an inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor (IMT). This is a locally aggressive neoplasm, and the most appropriate next step, given the incomplete initial surgery and the adherence noted intraoperatively, is to ensure complete local excision was achieved with clear margins. We should obtain the final surgical pathology report to confirm the margin status before deciding on any adjuvant therapy.
[AI Assistant]: I agree that the immunoprofile strongly supports an inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor (IMT). However, given the assessment that the confidence in this claim is currently low, we should consider the differential for spindle cell lesions in this location, such as a synovial sarcoma or a low-grade sarcoma, which can also express these markers. Let's review the pathology more closely, especially the ALK staining pattern and any molecular testing, to solidify the diagnosis before finalizing management.
[Doctor]: The differential you raise is reasonable, but the presentation, encapsulation, inflammatory cuff, and immunoprofile together are classic for IMT. We don't have molecular results, but ALK positivity with D5F3 clone in this context is highly specific. The critical next step remains confirming margin status from our own resection to guide further local management.
[AI Assistant]: You are correct that the combined features strongly point to IMT, and confirming margin status is indeed the immediate practical step. Given the lesion's adherence and prior recurrence, ensuring a complete resection with negative margins is paramount to prevent local relapse. We should await the final report on margins and then discuss the need for surveillance.
[Doctor]: Exactly. The final margin status report will dictate everything. If margins are clear, we can proceed with surveillance imaging. If involved or close, we need to discuss the feasibility and risks of re-excision versus close observation, given the tumor's low-grade histology and ALK positivity. We'll arrange that review.
[AI Assistant]: That's a sound plan. For a low-grade, ALK-positive IMT, a negative margin may allow for surveillance, while a positive margin warrants a multidisciplinary discussion weighing the morbidity of re-excision against the risk of recurrence, which is often indolent. Let's obtain that report and convene the tumor board.
[Doctor]: Agreed. We'll get the final margin report and then proceed with a tumor board discussion to formalize the surveillance or re-intervention plan. I'll set that in motion.
[AI Assistant]: Perfect. That's a prudent and collaborative approach. I'll be ready to assist with the tumor board discussion once the final pathology report is available.
[Doctor]: Agreed. I've already initiated the steps to convene the tumor board and will integrate the final margin report into our discussion. We have a clear, actionable plan.
[AI Assistant]: Excellent. This coordinated, multidisciplinary approach is ideal for managing a locally recurrent IMT. I look forward to reviewing the final report and contributing to the discussion.

case_info.explanation: Laryngeal histoplasmosis is a rare extrapulmonary manifestation ofHistoplasma capsulatum, a dimorphic fungus endemic to the Ohio and Mississippi river valleys. While histoplasmosis typically presents as a self-limited pulmonary illness, it may disseminate and affect extrapulmonary organs, including the larynx, even in immunocompetent individuals.1In this case, a man with no overt immunosuppression developed ulcerative supraglottic disease mimicking cancer, ultimately diagnosed by fungal staining on biopsy. Endoscopic features of laryngeal histoplasmosis can closely resemble squamous cell carcinoma, with ulcerative lesions, irregular mucosa, or masslike findings localized to the epiglottis, aryepiglottic folds, or vocal cords.2The overlap in appearance frequently leads to initial diagnostic concern for cancer, particularly in older adults with a history of tobacco use.3,4However, histopathologic evaluation remains the criterion standard for diagnosis. Histology results typically reveal necrotizing and nonnecrotizing granulomatous inflammation with multinucleated giant cells and fungal organisms.5,6Grocott methenamine silver or periodic acid–Schiff staining identifies the characteristic small, oval intracellular yeasts ofH capsulatum. In this case, the biopsy lacked dysplasia or neoplasia but demonstrated abundant submucosal nonnecrotizing granulomatous inflammation and multinucleated giant cell formation with fungal organisms consistent withH capsulatum. A serum histoplasma antigen level was then obtained and returned positive at 1.95 ng/mL, supporting the diagnosis and prompting antifungal therapy. Alternative considerations include laryngeal tuberculosis (TB), which may also present with hoarseness, mucosal ulceration, and granulomatous inflammation. However, TB is identified by acid-fast bacilli on staining or culture.4In this patient, no acid-fast bacilli were found, and fungal organisms were clearly demonstrated. Chronic laryngitis, another consideration in those who smoke, does not typically cause ulceration or granulomas and lacks fungal or mycobacterial organisms.1 Imaging studies are generally nonspecific but may support the extent of involvement. In this case, imaging was not diagnostic. The patient’s location in the Ohio River Valley served as an epidemiologic clue. Inhalation of microconidia from contaminated soil, often associated with bird or bat droppings, is the primary route of exposure.3While disseminated disease is more common in immunocompromised patients, it may also occur in older or chronically ill individuals without overt immunodeficiency. The treatment of laryngeal histoplasmosis is guided by the Infectious Diseases Society of America. For moderate to severe disease, the Infectious Diseases Society of America recommends liposomal amphotericin B at 3.0 mg/kg/d for 1 to 2 weeks, followed by oral itraconazole at 200 mg twice daily for at least 12 months.7For mild to moderate cases, itraconazole may be sufficient alone. In cases where immunosuppression cannot be reversed, long-term suppressive therapy may be necessary.8,9 This patient received a 2-week course of intravenous liposomal amphotericin B followed by a prolonged course of oral amphotericin B, as recommended by the infectious team. He also experienced 2 transient ischemic attacks during hospitalization, likely from a septic origin, and began anticoagulation with warfarin. His hoarseness and odynophagia improved considerably within 1 month. At 3-month follow-up, he remained symptom free. The initial delay in diagnosis underscores the importance of including fungal infections in the differential diagnosis of ulcerative laryngeal lesions, particularly in endemic areas. Laryngeal histoplasmosis is an important clinical mimic of squamous cell carcinoma and TB, and early biopsy with fungal staining is critical for accurate diagnosis. Prompt antifungal therapy can prevent complications such as airway obstruction, systemic dissemination, or unnecessary oncologic intervention. This case reinforces the need for clinicians to maintain suspicion for histoplasmosis in patients with chronic hoarseness and supraglottic lesions, even in the absence of overt immunosuppression.

case_info.explanation: Laryngeal histoplasmosis is a rare extrapulmonary manifestation ofHistoplasma capsulatum, a dimorphic fungus endemic to the Ohio and Mississippi river valleys. While histoplasmosis typically presents as a self-limited pulmonary illness, it may disseminate and affect extrapulmonary organs, including the larynx, even in immunocompetent individuals.1In this case, a man with no overt immunosuppression developed ulcerative supraglottic disease mimicking cancer, ultimately diagnosed by fungal staining on biopsy. Endoscopic features of laryngeal histoplasmosis can closely resemble squamous cell carcinoma, with ulcerative lesions, irregular mucosa, or masslike findings localized to the epiglottis, aryepiglottic folds, or vocal cords.2The overlap in appearance frequently leads to initial diagnostic concern for cancer, particularly in older adults with a history of tobacco use.3,4However, histopathologic evaluation remains the criterion standard for diagnosis. Histology results typically reveal necrotizing and nonnecrotizing granulomatous inflammation with multinucleated giant cells and fungal organisms.5,6Grocott methenamine silver or periodic acid–Schiff staining identifies the characteristic small, oval intracellular yeasts ofH capsulatum. In this case, the biopsy lacked dysplasia or neoplasia but demonstrated abundant submucosal nonnecrotizing granulomatous inflammation and multinucleated giant cell formation with fungal organisms consistent withH capsulatum. A serum histoplasma antigen level was then obtained and returned positive at 1.95 ng/mL, supporting the diagnosis and prompting antifungal therapy. Alternative considerations include laryngeal tuberculosis (TB), which may also present with hoarseness, mucosal ulceration, and granulomatous inflammation. However, TB is identified by acid-fast bacilli on staining or culture.4In this patient, no acid-fast bacilli were found, and fungal organisms were clearly demonstrated. Chronic laryngitis, another consideration in those who smoke, does not typically cause ulceration or granulomas and lacks fungal or mycobacterial organisms.1 Imaging studies are generally nonspecific but may support the extent of involvement. In this case, imaging was not diagnostic. The patient’s location in the Ohio River Valley served as an epidemiologic clue. Inhalation of microconidia from contaminated soil, often associated with bird or bat droppings, is the primary route of exposure.3While disseminated disease is more common in immunocompromised patients, it may also occur in older or chronically ill individuals without overt immunodeficiency. The treatment of laryngeal histoplasmosis is guided by the Infectious Diseases Society of America. For moderate to severe disease, the Infectious Diseases Society of America recommends liposomal amphotericin B at 3.0 mg/kg/d for 1 to 2 weeks, followed by oral itraconazole at 200 mg twice daily for at least 12 months.7For mild to moderate cases, itraconazole may be sufficient alone. In cases where immunosuppression cannot be reversed, long-term suppressive therapy may be necessary.8,9 This patient received a 2-week course of intravenous liposomal amphotericin B followed by a prolonged course of oral amphotericin B, as recommended by the infectious team. He also experienced 2 transient ischemic attacks during hospitalization, likely from a septic origin, and began anticoagulation with warfarin. His hoarseness and odynophagia improved considerably within 1 month. At 3-month follow-up, he remained symptom free. The initial delay in diagnosis underscores the importance of including fungal infections in the differential diagnosis of ulcerative laryngeal lesions, particularly in endemic areas. Laryngeal histoplasmosis is an important clinical mimic of squamous cell carcinoma and TB, and early biopsy with fungal staining is critical for accurate diagnosis. Prompt antifungal therapy can prevent complications such as airway obstruction, systemic dissemination, or unnecessary oncologic intervention. This case reinforces the need for clinicians to maintain suspicion for histoplasmosis in patients with chronic hoarseness and supraglottic lesions, even in the absence of overt immunosuppression.

case_info.explanation: Laryngeal histoplasmosis is a rare extrapulmonary manifestation ofHistoplasma capsulatum, a dimorphic fungus endemic to the Ohio and Mississippi river valleys. While histoplasmosis typically presents as a self-limited pulmonary illness, it may disseminate and affect extrapulmonary organs, including the larynx, even in immunocompetent individuals.1In this case, a man with no overt immunosuppression developed ulcerative supraglottic disease mimicking cancer, ultimately diagnosed by fungal staining on biopsy. Endoscopic features of laryngeal histoplasmosis can closely resemble squamous cell carcinoma, with ulcerative lesions, irregular mucosa, or masslike findings localized to the epiglottis, aryepiglottic folds, or vocal cords.2The overlap in appearance frequently leads to initial diagnostic concern for cancer, particularly in older adults with a history of tobacco use.3,4However, histopathologic evaluation remains the criterion standard for diagnosis. Histology results typically reveal necrotizing and nonnecrotizing granulomatous inflammation with multinucleated giant cells and fungal organisms.5,6Grocott methenamine silver or periodic acid–Schiff staining identifies the characteristic small, oval intracellular yeasts ofH capsulatum. In this case, the biopsy lacked dysplasia or neoplasia but demonstrated abundant submucosal nonnecrotizing granulomatous inflammation and multinucleated giant cell formation with fungal organisms consistent withH capsulatum. A serum histoplasma antigen level was then obtained and returned positive at 1.95 ng/mL, supporting the diagnosis and prompting antifungal therapy. Alternative considerations include laryngeal tuberculosis (TB), which may also present with hoarseness, mucosal ulceration, and granulomatous inflammation. However, TB is identified by acid-fast bacilli on staining or culture.4In this patient, no acid-fast bacilli were found, and fungal organisms were clearly demonstrated. Chronic laryngitis, another consideration in those who smoke, does not typically cause ulceration or granulomas and lacks fungal or mycobacterial organisms.1 Imaging studies are generally nonspecific but may support the extent of involvement. In this case, imaging was not diagnostic. The patient’s location in the Ohio River Valley served as an epidemiologic clue. Inhalation of microconidia from contaminated soil, often associated with bird or bat droppings, is the primary route of exposure.3While disseminated disease is more common in immunocompromised patients, it may also occur in older or chronically ill individuals without overt immunodeficiency. The treatment of laryngeal histoplasmosis is guided by the Infectious Diseases Society of America. For moderate to severe disease, the Infectious Diseases Society of America recommends liposomal amphotericin B at 3.0 mg/kg/d for 1 to 2 weeks, followed by oral itraconazole at 200 mg twice daily for at least 12 months.7For mild to moderate cases, itraconazole may be sufficient alone. In cases where immunosuppression cannot be reversed, long-term suppressive therapy may be necessary.8,9 This patient received a 2-week course of intravenous liposomal amphotericin B followed by a prolonged course of oral amphotericin B, as recommended by the infectious team. He also experienced 2 transient ischemic attacks during hospitalization, likely from a septic origin, and began anticoagulation with warfarin. His hoarseness and odynophagia improved considerably within 1 month. At 3-month follow-up, he remained symptom free. The initial delay in diagnosis underscores the importance of including fungal infections in the differential diagnosis of ulcerative laryngeal lesions, particularly in endemic areas. Laryngeal histoplasmosis is an important clinical mimic of squamous cell carcinoma and TB, and early biopsy with fungal staining is critical for accurate diagnosis. Prompt antifungal therapy can prevent complications such as airway obstruction, systemic dissemination, or unnecessary oncologic intervention. This case reinforces the need for clinicians to maintain suspicion for histoplasmosis in patients with chronic hoarseness and supraglottic lesions, even in the absence of overt immunosuppression.
